priceHiddenNote: Prices are quoted with the container and the delivery together, so the figure you get is the whole cost to your address rather than a headline that grows later. Ring 1300 467 776 or send the form and you will have a price for the exact unit.
disclaimer: Every figure on this page is a starting price in Australian dollars, before GST, for the grade named beside it. Where it finally lands depends on the individual unit, what is physically standing in stock that week, and which yard the container has to be released from — Cornubia, or one of the depots at Gympie, Rockhampton, Mackay, Townsville, Cairns, Grafton, Darwin or Fremantle. Nothing here becomes a quote until we have worked out the run to your address.
asIsNote: Grade is what decides whether the box keeps water out. Anything sold as cargo-worthy is inspected wind and watertight before release — for storage use, which is separate from the CSC certification an export job needs — and new single-trip units, one loaded voyage with rubbers that have barely weathered, are sealed as well. As-is is the cheap end and carries no watertight claim at all: expect a previous repair, a floor section that has gone soft, or a gasket that no longer pulls up hard against the frame. We list those faults and photograph them on request, before delivery, so nothing turns up as a surprise when the truck does. If what goes inside has to stay dry, start at cargo-worthy.
gradeNote: Three grades cover nearly everything we move. The money between the top and the bottom of that range is usually larger than the gap between two yards quoting on the same grade, so settle the grade first and treat it as the only fair basis for comparing anybody's price.

grades.name: New (single-trip)
grades.blurb: Manufactured, packed once, sailed once, then stripped out at this end. Walls true, floor clean, factory paint, rubbers that have seen almost no weather. Appearance varies from batch to batch — colour, markings and the odd handling scuff — so ask what is on the ground. Where the container will be on show or converted, start here.

grades.name: Cargo-worthy used
grades.blurb: A used unit that is structurally sound, with a solid floor and doors that seal. Scuffs, patches of surface rust and faded shipping-line livery come with it. Inspected wind and watertight before release, for storage use — current CSC certification for shipping is a separate matter and is checked on the specific unit if you need it. This is what most buyers should be looking at, and it is the bulk of what leaves the Cornubia yard.

grades.name: As-is
grades.blurb: Finished with sea service and priced on its faults. Cheapest by a distance, and perfectly serviceable for plenty of jobs — a locked store under an existing roof, the shell of a site office, the base of a build. Not sold watertight, and not a sealed vessel either. The faults on the individual unit get described plainly and photographed on request before it goes anywhere near a truck.

sizes.name: 10ft Containers
sizes.title: 10ft Shipping Containers
sizes.lead: The size that gets a phone call when the block is pinched and the fence sits closer than anybody would like. A ten is not usually a shortened twenty, whatever the assumption — most leave the factory at that length or are built short deliberately, which is why it is rarely the cheap option per cubic metre.
sizes.pickIf: Side access is pinched, the setback leaves nothing to manoeuvre in, or all that is needed is a lockable spot for the mower, an air compressor and a wall of hand tools.
sizes.fits: A ride-on, a bench and shelving up the walls — roughly what a single lock-up garage swallows. A two-bedroom unit's worth of furniture will go in if it is packed hard and nothing in it is fragile.
why: Slips past the side of an ordinary suburban home where a twenty has no chance. On a standard side passage that fact alone usually settles the argument.
Comes off an ordinary tilt-tray and wants about half the approach a twenty needs, so a lot of sites that would otherwise fail become workable.

Usually works out dearer per cubic metre than a twenty, because supply is thin and the build is not simply a cut-down box. Where there is room for the longer box, ask for both figures before deciding, and you will hear which one suits from us rather than an easy yes.
sizes.watch: Ten-footers are the tightest supply of any size in the country. Used ones can turn over inside a week, so a figure somebody gave you last month may not hold today. Ring and ask what is physically standing at Cornubia, or at whichever depot is nearest you.
sizes.access: A ten lands off a standard tilt-tray and wants roughly half the approach a twenty does — around 12 metres of straight run, 3 metres clear where it pinches, and 4.5 metres overhead while the tray tips. That is precisely why the size exists. Tight suburban blocks, pinched side passages and awkward courtyards in the inner city become workable at this length and stay impossible at anything longer.
sizes.seoTitle: 10ft Shipping Containers For Sale & Hire | Koala Containers
sizes.seoDesc: 10ft shipping containers for sale and hire Australia-wide. A 10 foot unit goes where a 20ft cannot. Ask what is standing in the yard — 1300 467 776.
sizes.h1: 10ft Shipping Containers — Buy Or Hire, Australia-Wide

depth.h: Is a 10 foot container big enough for the job?
p: The cubic figure flatters it. 15.9m³ sounds generous until you allow for reaching things, and the honest comparison is a single lock-up garage bay at full container height — about 2.39m of clear headroom, which is more than most garages give you. That height is where a 10ft quietly wins: shelving to the roof, a ride-on underneath, and a bench along one wall still leaves a walkway.

Pallets are the test that settles most arguments. Two Australian standard pallets sit across the width of a 10ft with very little to spare, and the door opening is 2.34m wide by 2.28m high, so anything long or awkward has to swing in through that gap rather than appear inside by magic. Measure the longest thing you own before you settle the length. The full figures, alongside the 20ft and 40ft, are on the [container dimensions page](/dimensions/).

depth.h: 10ft or 20ft — where the ten actually wins, and where it does not
p: A 10ft is not the cheap way to buy room, and we would rather say so than sell you the wrong box. Ten-footers are built short deliberately rather than cut down from a twenty, supply of them is the thinnest of any size in the country, and the result is that you almost always pay more per cubic metre than you would for a [20ft shipping container](/20ft-shipping-containers/). If the ground will take the longer unit, the longer unit is usually the better buy.

What a 10ft buys you is access, and access is not a nice-to-have. It slips down the side passage of an ordinary suburban house where a twenty has no chance, it comes off a standard tilt-tray rather than needing a crane, and it wants roughly half the straight approach. On a pinched block, a short setback or an inner-city courtyard, that is the difference between having a container and not having one. It is also the sensible pick when the job is genuinely small — a lock-up for the mower, the compressor and a wall of hand tools, or a secure store on a site with no shed.

Ring with the address and a description of the entry and you will get both figures side by side, the ten and the twenty, with the delivery worked into each. Where the twenty fits, we will tell you it fits.

depth.h: Siting a 10ft on a tight block
p: A 10ft weighs about 1,300 kg empty and puts that load through four corner castings rather than spreading it across the footprint, so what sits under those four corners matters more than the ground in between. Concrete pavers, sleepers or short concrete pads at each corner are the usual answer. Level it properly before it is loaded, because doors that shut sweetly on a level box will bind on a twisted one and no amount of adjusting the locking bars fixes a racked frame.

Leave yourself room in front of the doors. They swing through a wide arc and need roughly 2.5m of clear ground to open fully, which is the detail most often discovered after the truck has gone. Keep the unit off a fence line if you can, give the roof somewhere to drain, and if it is going on grass or soil, expect the corners to sink unevenly through a wet season unless they are bearing on something solid.

Access at the street end is a separate question, and it is the one that decides which truck comes. There is more on it, including what to photograph before you enquire, on the [delivery and access page](/delivery/).

Yes, and that is one of the quieter arguments for the size. A ten is the easiest container in the range to relocate because it goes back onto an ordinary tilt-tray, so a move within a property, across town or to a new address is a straightforward job rather than a crane booking. Plenty of people buy a 10ft precisely because it is not a permanent decision.

The catch is that it has to come out the way it went in. If a fence panel came down, a tree was trimmed or a slab was still being poured on delivery day, the same clearances have to exist again on the way out. Empty it before it moves — a loaded container is not a container that can be dragged — and if it has been sitting on soil for a few years, allow time to get it lifted clear rather than winched. A container that has been modified with a roller door, windows or lining moves just as easily; [modification work](/container-modifications/) does not lock it in place.

depth.h: Grades on a 10ft, and what each one promises
p: The grade decides more than the length ever will. New single-trip means one loaded voyage, rubbers that have barely weathered and a floor nothing has been dropped on. Cargo-worthy used is the volume grade and is inspected wind and watertight before it is released, which is a storage standard and separate from the CSC certification an export job needs. As-is is the cheap end and carries no watertight claim at all — expect a previous repair, a soft section of floor or a gasket that no longer pulls up hard against the frame.

Because 10ft supply is so thin, what is available in a given grade moves week to week far more than it does on a twenty. A figure somebody quoted last month may not hold today, and the useful question is not what a list says but what is physically standing at Cornubia or at the depot nearest your address. Ring and you will be told exactly that. The grade descriptions in full are on the [container grades page](/container-grades/), and if you would rather not own it at all, a 10ft can go out on [container hire](/shipping-container-hire/) by the week.

Koala sells and hires 10ft containers in every state and territory, and your unit is released from the yard closest to your address rather than carted across the country to get to you. That is worth something real on a size this scarce: a ten that is not in one yard is often standing in another, and the network is wide enough that the answer to “can you get one” is usually yes rather than a wait.

Our own yard is at 51–55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, south of Brisbane, and you are welcome to walk in and look at a unit any weekday. If the drive is not worth making, photographs of the exact container are sent through on request, before delivery. For local detail, start with [Brisbane](/brisbane/), the [Gold Coast](/gold-coast/), [Sydney](/sydney/), [Melbourne](/melbourne/), [Perth](/perth/) or [Toowoomba](/toowoomba/).

extraFaqs.q: Is a 10 foot container the same as a 10ft shipping container?
extraFaqs.a: Same thing. “10ft”, “10 foot” and “ten-footer” all describe a container about 2.99m long externally, and the trade uses the three interchangeably. The measurement is nominal and taken from the outside, which is why the inside comes back at 2.83m rather than a round three metres.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between a 10ft and a 20ft shipping container?
extraFaqs.a: Length, and almost nothing else. Both are 2.44m wide and 2.59m high externally, both take the same doors, the same locking bars and the same lock box, and both come in the same grades. A 20ft is roughly double the floor area, takes about ten Australian standard pallets on the floor against two across the width of a ten, and is usually cheaper per cubic metre because supply of twenties is deep and supply of tens is not. A 10ft goes onto a tilt-tray and wants about half the approach, which is the whole reason to choose one.

extraFaqs.q: Can I move a 10ft shipping container after it has been delivered?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. A 10ft is the easiest size in the range to relocate because it goes back onto a standard tilt-tray rather than needing a crane. Empty it first, and make sure the access that got it in still exists — if a fence came down or a tree was trimmed on delivery day, the same clearances are needed on the way out.

It depends entirely on the grade. New single-trip and cargo-worthy used units are inspected wind and watertight before they are released, for storage use. As-is units are not sold watertight and carry no such claim — they are the cheap end precisely because something on them is past its best, and we will ask what is going inside before letting anybody buy one on price alone. If the contents have to stay dry, start at cargo-worthy.

extraFaqs.q: How much room do I need to open the doors on a 10ft?
extraFaqs.a: About 2.5m of clear ground in front of the doors for them to swing through their full arc, plus somewhere to stand while you load. It is the measurement people forget, because the truck fits and the container fits and then the doors meet a fence. Check it before you decide where the box lands, not after.

sizes.name: 20ft Containers
sizes.title: 20ft Shipping Containers
sizes.seoTitle: 20ft Shipping Containers For Sale & Hire | Koala Containers
sizes.seoDesc: 20ft shipping containers for sale and hire Australia-wide. 6.06m long, 33.2m³ inside, in new, cargo-worthy and as-is grades. Priced with delivery.
sizes.lead: The default, and usually the correct default. The whole industry is built around this length — the deepest stock, the widest choice of grade, and no drama at all getting a truck underneath one.
sizes.pickIf: There is about seven metres of straight, reasonably level ground for it to sit on, and you would rather not discover in half a year that the bigger box was the answer.
sizes.fits: The contents of a three-bedroom house, packed with some thought. Or a complete trade fit-out — racking along one wall, a bench across the end, and enough floor left to walk in and pull one thing out without emptying the front half first.
why: The deepest supply of any size, week in and week out, so you get to choose a grade rather than accept whatever has turned up. What it costs depends on the grade and the delivery run, and it is quoted for the unit.
Goes on and off a standard tilt-tray. Wants around 20 metres of straight approach and 3.5 metres of width where the drive narrows, which most suburban and rural blocks can manage.
Sits inside most council rules for a temporary or secondary structure without argument. Ring your council anyway — the requirements genuinely vary from one shire to the next.
sizes.watch: The regret we hear most often comes from somebody who bought a twenty and wanted a forty. A pair of twenties generally costs more than one forty and arrives on two separate trucks. If there is any prospect of the job growing, get a price on the forty before you decide — on current quotes a 40ft often costs only a little more than a 20ft for about twice the volume, though it always comes down to the grade, the unit and the run.
sizes.access: Around 20 metres of straight approach, 3.5 metres of width where the drive narrows, and 4.5 metres of clearance above while the tray is raised. Most blocks, suburban or rural, can find that much, which is part of why this length is the standard answer. What catches people is getting back out again: a long drive with no turning circle means the truck reverses the full length of it to the road.

sizes.name: 40ft Containers
sizes.title: 40ft Shipping Containers
sizes.seoTitle: 40ft Shipping Containers For Sale & Hire | Koala Containers
sizes.seoDesc: 40ft shipping containers for sale and hire Australia-wide. 12.19m long, 67.7m³ inside, in new, cargo-worthy and as-is grades. Priced with delivery.
sizes.lead: Double the length and near enough double the room. On current quotes a used forty often costs only a little more than a used twenty, so where the site takes it, it is usually the most room per dollar — but that depends on the grade, the unit and the delivery run, and it is never the container that decides. It is whether a truck can get in, and whether the ground will let the thing lie flat.
sizes.pickIf: You have the space, the approach is genuinely open, and you want the most storage per dollar the site will allow.
sizes.fits: A big house plus the contents of the shed, or a proper workshop with an aisle down the centre to work in. Frequently bought two at a time and stood parallel, with a roof spanning the gap to make a covered bay.
why: Often only a little more than a used twenty for about twice the volume on current quotes. Grade and the delivery run move that, so ask for both figures rather than assuming.
One truck instead of two, one lot of cartage instead of two, one prepared footing instead of two.
Mates and stacks neatly with a second forty, which is what makes the twin-container covered bay such a common build.
sizes.watch: Everything hinges on access at this length. Reckon on 30 metres of straight approach, 4 metres of width at the tightest point, nothing hanging over any of it, and ground firm enough that four corner castings will not sink into it. A side loader manages tighter ground than a tilt-tray; on most side loaders the container comes off the driver's side of the trailer, so the direction of approach matters and the carrier confirms it on the day. Send three photos through and we will give you an answer before anybody prices it.
sizes.access: Reckon on 30 metres of straight approach, 4 metres of width at the tightest point, and nothing overhanging any part of the run. A side loader copes with a good deal less room than a tilt-tray, but on most side loaders the container comes off the driver's side of the trailer — so the direction the truck can come in from tends to dictate which side of the block the box can end up on. The site and the carrier decide which truck it is; settle that well before delivery day.

types.name: General Purpose
types.title: General Purpose Shipping Containers
types.lead: The plain box, and the right call about eight times out of ten. Corrugated Corten steel, plywood floor over steel bearers, a pair of cargo doors at one end, easy to get a forklift into, and sealed overhead against rain once you are at cargo-worthy grade or above.
types.metaDesc: General purpose shipping containers for sale and hire Australia-wide in 10ft, 20ft and 40ft. New, cargo-worthy and as-is grades from Koala Containers.
points: New single-trip and sound used units in 10ft, 20ft and 40ft
Cargo-worthy stock inspected wind and watertight before it leaves the depot
As-is is cheaper again and carries no watertight claim — we list the faults up front rather than let the truck deliver a surprise
Lock box welded on so bolt cutters cannot reach the padlock shackle
Photos of the actual unit on request, sent before delivery
detail: Externally a general purpose container measures 2.59m to the top rail, which leaves roughly 2.39m of clear height inside. Enough to stand a bay of pallet racking under and walk about beneath it without stooping. It is not enough for a mezzanine, and it is mean on head clearance if a roller door is going in and a forklift has to drive through it with a load raised. Where either of those is on the plan, price a high cube — the extra 300mm is cheaper than most people expect.

The floor is 28mm marine-grade ply sitting on steel cross-members, and it is routinely the part buyers pay least attention to. It carries a forklift and it carries a pallet jack. It is also what gives out first in a container that has spent years hauling something damp, so on used stock the floor is what gets looked at first and photographed first.

Doors are where the rest of the wear shows up. Two leaves at one end, four bars to lock them down, and a rubber gasket running right around the frame. Wind and watertight, when somebody inspects for it, is mostly a judgement about whether that gasket seats and whether the bars drag the doors up tight against it.

types.name: High Cube
types.title: High Cube Shipping Containers
types.lead: Identical footprint to a standard container with another foot of height on top — 2.90m to the rail rather than 2.59m. It reads as a trivial difference on paper and stops being trivial the moment you are standing inside one.
types.metaDesc: High cube shipping containers, sale and hire — an extra 300mm of internal height in 20ft and 40ft, delivered Australia-wide by Koala Containers.
points: 300mm more clear height inside, with the length and width unchanged
Offered in 20ft and 40ft, new single-trip or cargo-worthy used
The one to buy if the container is being lined, converted or fitted with a roller door
Designed to mate and stack with other high cubes; mixing heights in one stack is generally avoided and needs a competent assessment of the units involved
Black and yellow hatching along the top rail makes them easy to pick out on site
detail: The argument for a high cube is entirely about what the extra 300mm buys. Enough room to line walls and ceiling and still stand upright underneath. Clearance for a roller door a forklift can drive under with the tynes up. Depth enough to hang a mezzanine across one end. Attempt any of those inside a standard container and every one of them ends up a compromise.

The costs are genuine but modest. A high cube runs a little dearer than the standard version of the same length, and it stands 300mm taller on the trailer — which matters under a carport, beneath a branch, or through a gateway with a beam across the top. Measure the height at every point the truck has to pass, not simply the width.

One thing worth settling before buying a pair: mixing heights in a stack is generally avoided. The corner castings line up, but whether a particular high cube can safely sit on a particular standard box depends on the units, the base and the loads, and it wants a competent assessment rather than an assumption. If stacking is even a possibility later on, buy both at the same height now.

types.name: Side Opening
types.title: Side Opening Shipping Containers
types.lead: A container with doors running the full length of one side on top of the usual pair at the end. Nothing ends up buried behind anything else, every pallet position is reachable from outside, and a forklift can pull any one of them without shifting the rest.
types.metaDesc: Side opening shipping containers, sale and hire across Australia — doors down the whole side so a forklift can reach every pallet position.
points: Doors along the whole of one side, plus the standard pair at the end
New in 20ft and 40ft; used side openers surface rarely and sell fast
Turns the container from a tunnel into a shelf you can work from outside
Needs clear, level ground alongside the doors, so where the container can stand changes
Considerably dearer than a general purpose unit, and worth every cent on the right job
detail: Access is the only reason to pay the difference. In an ordinary container whatever you want is behind whatever went in first, and in practice that means dragging half the load onto the ground to reach it. A side opener does away with that completely. For a workshop, a parts store, a hire yard or anywhere stock cycles quickly, it changes the way the container gets used every day of the week.

Siting works differently and this is where people come unstuck. The leaves swing outwards across the full length, so allow about three metres of clear, flat standing along that side, and settle which way the container faces before the truck arrives. Spinning one around afterwards is another delivery. Decide which side the doors face, say so when you order, and the driver will land it that way round.

They are heavier and structurally more complicated than a plain box, so they cost more and there are simply fewer of them in circulation. Used examples do exist but they are uncommon — if one is wanted, say so early and we will keep an eye out rather than wait for one to appear.

types.name: Refrigerated
types.title: Refrigerated Shipping Containers
types.lead: Reefers — insulated panels all round, a stainless or aluminium interior, a T-bar deck for airflow, and an integral refrigeration unit built into one end. Two quite different products get sold under the one name, and that distinction matters more than any other decision on this page.
types.metaDesc: Refrigerated shipping containers and insulated coolroom shells for sale and hire — 20ft and 40ft reefers with integral units. Australia-wide delivery.
points: 20ft and 40ft units with the refrigeration machinery built into the front wall
Around 100mm of foamed panel through the walls, roof and floor, over a T-bar deck
A running reefer needs three-phase power at the site — 415V, and generally a dedicated outlet
Non-operating units sell cheaper and make an excellent insulated shell for a coolroom or a cellar
Photos of the unit and its machinery on request, sent before delivery
detail: Two products share the name. A running reefer has working refrigeration and will hold a set point, chilled or frozen, so long as it is plugged into three-phase power. A non-operating unit — the trade calls them NOR, or simply insulated boxes — is the same insulated shell with the machinery either dead or stripped out, sold as a cheap and extremely well-insulated room. A great many buyers only ever wanted the second one. Working out which of the two the job needs before you ring saves a serious amount of money.

Power is the part that catches people. A reefer draws three phases and it draws them continuously rather than in a polite little cycle, and it wants a supply and an outlet sized for the load. On a rural block or a new estate that can mean a sparky and a switchboard upgrade before the container earns a cent. Sort the supply out first — a reefer standing on a slab with nothing to plug into is an insulated shed with an expensive lump bolted to the front of it.

Once the unit is on your ground the machinery is yours to run and yours to look after. Refrigeration plant is serviced by refrigeration mechanics, it wants gas, filters and a periodic look at the controller, and any warranty on the plant sits with its manufacturer rather than with us on a used unit. We will tell you what a particular machine has done and whether it was pulled down under load before it left. Beyond that, running it and servicing it belong to the owner.

types.name: Dangerous Goods
types.title: Dangerous Goods Shipping Containers
types.lead: Storage built from the outset for flammable liquids and other dangerous goods — a bunded floor, ventilation high and low, internal shelving, and the compliance plate a workplace inspector will want to read.
types.metaDesc: Dangerous goods containers for sale and hire — bunded floor, engineered ventilation, certified to the relevant Australian Standard. Australia-wide.
points: Bunded sump floor sized to hold a spill inside the container instead of on your ground
Engineered ventilation high and low, hazard placarding and a compliance plate
Built and certified to the Australian Standard covering the class being stored
Available in 10ft and 20ft, to buy or to hire
Not a general purpose box with a label stuck on it — a DG unit differs from the floor up
detail: A dangerous goods unit is a different container, not a modified one. The floor is a sealed bund sized to retain a proportion of what is stored should a drum split, the ventilation is designed rather than incidental, the fit-out inside is non-sparking, and a plate on the unit states exactly what it was constructed to. That plate is the document an inspector or an insurer asks to see.

Which standard applies comes down to what is going inside it. Flammable liquids, corrosives, oxidising agents and toxics each carry their own requirements, and a unit certified for one class is not automatically acceptable for another. Give us the class and the volume ahead of anything else — those two facts choose the container.

Nearly everybody enquiring about one already has a compliance date behind them. Mention it when you ring. DG units are more often built to order than found standing in a yard, and lead times run longer than a plain container, so the deadline shapes the answer as much as the specification does.

conditions.name: New (Single-Trip)
conditions.title: New Shipping Containers
conditions.lead: A new container has been built, loaded once, carried one voyage and opened up at this end. That single trip is why the trade says one-tripper rather than new, and it is the only honest description — a container that had genuinely never carried anything would still be sitting outside the factory.
conditions.metaDesc: New single-trip shipping containers for sale — true walls, clean floors, factory paint, checked wind and watertight. 10ft, 20ft and 40ft nationally.
points: One loaded voyage, then straight into the yard — walls true, floor clean, paint barely weathered
Checked wind and watertight before release, the same as cargo-worthy stock
Available in 10ft, 20ft and 40ft, standard height or high cube
Usually offered in the factory colour of the run, so ask what is on the ground before settling on a shade
The right starting point where the container will be converted, lined, or seen from the street
detail: What you are paying for is the condition of the steel and the rubber. A one-trip unit has square corners, doors that swing without persuasion, and gaskets that have not spent a decade baking in the sun. On any container it is the doors and the seals that go first, so starting from new buys time before either becomes a job you have to think about. Like any steel box left outside it will still weather, and appearance varies from batch to batch.

It also matters where the container will be looked at. A cargo-worthy unit wears the marks of its working life and most buyers do not mind at all. Put one at the front of an acreage block, behind a shopfront, or on a site a client walks past every day, and suddenly the paint matters. New is the answer when appearance is part of the brief.

For conversions there is a further reason. Cutting a doorway or a window into a container that already carries patched repairs, filler or a wavy side wall makes the fabricator's job harder and the finish worse. Anybody doing a fit-out will thank you for handing them a straight box to start from.
conditions.bestFor: Conversions and fit-outs, display and customer-facing sites, long-term storage of anything that must stay dry, and buyers who want the longest run before doors or seals need attention.
conditions.watch: Single-trip stock arrives in batches and the colour varies from one run to the next. If you are matching an existing container or want a particular shade, ask what is actually available before you settle on it, and be ready to wait for the next arrival.

conditions.name: Cargo-Worthy Used
conditions.title: Used Shipping Containers
conditions.lead: Used covers a lot of ground, which is why it gets graded. Cargo-worthy is the line worth knowing: a structurally sound container with a solid floor and sealing doors, inspected and confirmed wind and watertight before it goes on a truck — for storage use. If you need to ship in it, current CSC certification is a separate check on the specific unit. Below cargo-worthy sits as-is, which is a different proposition entirely and priced accordingly.
conditions.metaDesc: Used shipping containers for sale — cargo-worthy grade inspected wind and watertight; as-is units cheaper and not sold watertight. 10ft to 40ft.
points: Cargo-worthy units inspected wind and watertight before they leave
Surface rust, dents and faded shipping-line paint are normal at this grade and do not affect the seal
As-is is a separate, cheaper grade and is not sold watertight
Floors and door gaskets are what we check first and photograph first
Photos of the actual unit on request, sent before delivery
detail: Most people should be buying at this grade. A cargo-worthy twenty does the same storage job as a new one, keeps the weather off just as well, and leaves a substantial sum in your pocket. The trade-off is cosmetic: expect faded livery, square patches where a shipping line painted over its own logo, dents through the side walls, and a floor that has obviously carried things.

Two things decide whether a used container is any good, and they are the floor and the doors. A floor that has carried something wet for years goes soft between the cross-members and you can feel it underfoot before you can see it. Gaskets perish, and once one has taken a set it will not pull up against the frame however hard the bars are cranked. Both get checked before a unit is released and both get photographed.

As-is deserves saying plainly. It has finished its working life at sea, it is priced on its faults, it is not sold watertight, and a given unit may carry a patched repair, a soft section of floor, or a seal that no longer seats. For a lock-up under an existing roof, a site shell or the base of a build it is often exactly the right buy. For anything that has to stay dry, it is not.
conditions.bestFor: General storage, site security, farm and trade use, hire fleets, and anyone who wants the container to work rather than to look new.
conditions.watch: Two cargo-worthy containers standing side by side can be a long way apart in condition and both still be honestly graded. Ask for photos of the specific unit on request before delivery rather than assuming the grade alone tells you everything about it.

conditions.name: Refurbished
conditions.title: Refurbished Shipping Containers
conditions.lead: A refurbished container is a used unit that has been repaired where it needed repairing and repainted in one colour. It looks a great deal better than it did, and done properly it is a sound buy — provided you understand what a coat of paint fixes and what it only covers over.
conditions.metaDesc: Refurbished shipping containers for sale — repaired, prepped and repainted in one colour. Straight answers on what a repaint fixes and what it hides.
points: Rust ground back or cut out, repairs welded in, then prepped and painted in a single colour
Doors rehung and perished gaskets renewed as part of the work
Ends up uniform, which matters where several containers stand together on one site
Paint over unprepared steel is cosmetic only — ask what was done underneath before it was painted
Refurbished describes the work, not a certification; the grade underneath still applies
detail: Done properly the sequence is repair first and paint last. Perforated steel is cut out and new plate welded in, surface rust is ground back to bright metal, the floor is checked and sections replaced where it has softened, gaskets that have taken a set are renewed, and only then is the container prepped and painted. Every one of those steps costs money, and every one of them becomes invisible the moment the colour goes on.

Which is exactly why the question to ask is what happened before the paint. A repaint over live rust looks identical on the day it lands and will bubble through in a season or two. Ask whether steel was replaced, whether the floor was touched, whether the gaskets are new. A yard that has done the work will happily tell you, and the answer is worth more than the photographs.

It is worth being clear about what refurbishment is not, as well. Repainting does not lift the grade. A unit that was not watertight beforehand does not become watertight because it is now one colour. Where the container has to keep rain off what goes inside it, that has to be established on the condition of the unit and confirmed, never inferred from how tidy it looks.
conditions.bestFor: Front-of-house storage, sites where several containers stand together and ought to match, rental and hire fleets, and anyone who wants a used price with a presentable finish.
conditions.watch: A uniform colour makes containers hard to compare by eye, and that cuts both ways. Judge a refurbished unit on the floor, the doors and the seals exactly as you would judge any used one, and ask for photos on request before delivery.

mods.name: Personnel Doors
mods.blurb: A hinged steel door cut into the side or the end so the container can be walked into without swinging the cargo doors open. A frame is welded into the cut, then a lockset and generally a closer. Worth doing wherever the container is opened daily, or where the big doors face into the weather.

mods.name: Windows
mods.blurb: Sliding or awning windows framed into the wall, most often with a security grille or bars and a flyscreen behind. Placement decides how useful the container is afterwards, so mark them out before anyone cuts. A window in the wrong wall costs you the shelving position or the racking run that would have gone there.

mods.name: Roller Doors
mods.blurb: A roller shutter fitted into one end or one side, giving a wide clear opening you can drive a forklift straight through. Head clearance decides the job: on a standard container the drum eats into an opening that was already tight, so most roller door conversions are better done in a high cube.

mods.name: Insulation and Lining
mods.blurb: Foam or batt insulation packed between a timber or steel frame and sheeted over in ply, villaboard or colour-backed steel. It cuts the internal temperature swing sharply and stops condensation forming on bare steel overhead. Expect to lose 50 to 75mm off every internal dimension, which is another reason lined jobs tend to start with a high cube.

mods.name: Shelving and Racking
mods.blurb: Steel shelving bolted or welded to the side walls, or freestanding pallet racking set down on the floor. Wall-mounted shelving keeps the floor clear and suits hand-loaded stock. Racking suits pallets and forklifts but needs the aisle width to work in. Decide how the container will be loaded first and the layout follows from that.

mods.name: Ventilation
mods.blurb: Whirlybirds through the roof, louvred vents in the walls, or both together. A sealed container holds warm damp air, condensation forms overhead and it drips back down onto whatever is stored underneath. Cross-flow ventilation is the cheapest answer to that, and it matters most in humid coastal areas and through the northern wet season.
